newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba says it would grant asylum to Peru rebels.
newsitem.headline: Cuba says it would grant asylum to Peru rebels.

text.p: Cuba confirmed on Thursday it had accepted a formal request from Japan to grant asylum to Peruvian Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima if there was a negotiated settlement to the 93-day crisis.
The ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma said visiting Japanese Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura delivered Japan's request in a meeting on Wednesday evening with President Fidel Castro.

"Komura carries an official request from the Japanese government for Cuba to receive, for humanitarian reasons, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) group that are occupying the Japanese embassy in Lima," the newspaper said.
"The Cuban government ratified its willingess to cooperate where possible in the solution to the situation, on the basis of an agreement between the involved parties," the newspaper added.
Earlier in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said Komura delivered a personal appeal to Castro from the prime minister asking for asylum for hostage-takers.
"I hope this will accelerate moves to seek an early solution," Hashimoto told reporters in Tokyo.

Other than a Granma newspaper report on the meeting between Castro and Komura, there was no comment by Cuban government officials on what was discussed. But Japanese government sources in Tokyo said Castro emphasised that Cuba viewed its offer as a humanitarian gesture.
"Our acceptance on this issue is from a humanitarian point of view. Cuba is not a country to take in terrorism," the sources quoted Castro as saying.
Castro earlier this month told Peru's President Alberto Fujimori that Cuba was willing to take in the hostage-takers, saying Havana viewed this as a "moral duty."
Following Fujimori's trip to Havana, the rebels told reporters they wanted to stay in Peru but said they reserved comment on the possibility of asylum in Cuba.
The rebels burst into a cocktail party at the ambassador's home on Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of hostages, but have eventually released all but 72.

The careful wording of the Granma report on the meeting between Komura and Castro reflected Cuba's caution on the affair from the outset. While the MRTA are said to be inspired by Cuba's revolution, Havana for weeks declined comment on the affair, saying only that it wanted to see a peaceful solution.

Castro's government waited to be asked by Fujimori before offering possible asylum to the rebels, and insisted at that time that all parties involved would have to be in formal agreement if such a move took place.
There would be precedents if the rebels were to eventually come to the communist-ruled island.
Castro mediated in June 1995 to secure freedom for the kidnapped brother of former Colombian president Cesar Gaviria. Some of the kidnappers and their families flew to Cuba.
Havana also intervened to help resolve a crisis in Colombia in 1980 when guerrillas of the M-19 movement seized 14 ambassadors at the Dominican Embassy residence in Bogota.
